title: SLI, SLO and SLA
summary:
Three layers, each built on the one before:

- **SLI (Service Level Indicator):** a *metric* that measures how the service behaves for users, expressed as a ratio of good events to valid events: "fraction of requests that return non-5xx", "fraction served in under 300 ms".
- **SLO (Service Level Objective):** an SLI plus a **target** plus a **time window**: "99.9% of requests succeed, measured over a rolling 30 days". It is an internal goal that steers engineering decisions.
- **SLA (Service Level Agreement):** a **contract** with customers that attaches consequences (credits, refunds, termination rights) if a level is missed. SLAs are deliberately looser than the SLO behind them, so you notice and react before you owe money.

The target implies an **error budget**: with 99.9%, 0.1% of events (about 43 minutes of full outage per 30 days) may fail. Spend it on deploys and experiments; when it is gone, slow down and fix reliability. Alert on the **burn rate** of the budget rather than on single failures.

Choose SLIs from the **user's** view and use percentiles for latency: an average hides the slow tail that real users feel, and a healthy server CPU says nothing about whether requests succeeded. Related: [load shedding](#/sd/f/load-shedding), timeouts and retries are the mechanisms that defend an SLO under stress.

drills.q: Which statement is an SLO rather than an SLI or an SLA?
options: Fraction of HTTP requests answered with non-5xx status
99.9% of requests succeed, measured over a rolling 30-day window
If monthly availability falls below 99.5%, the customer receives a 10% credit
p99 latency of the checkout endpoint in milliseconds
drills.explain: An SLO combines an indicator, a target (99.9%) and a window (30 days). The first and last are SLIs (just metrics); the credit clause is an SLA because it carries a contractual consequence.

drills.q: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over a 30-day window, measured as time with full outage. How many minutes of full outage fit in the error budget? (30 days = 43,200 minutes)
drills.explain: The budget is 0.1% of the window: 43,200 × 0.001 = 43.2 minutes. Going from 99.9% to 99.99% shrinks it tenfold to about 4.3 minutes, which is why each extra nine costs far more engineering than the last.

drills.q: A request-based SLO requires 99.95% of requests to succeed in a window. The service handles 10,000,000 requests in that window. How many failed requests can it afford?
drills.explain: The allowed failure fraction is 100% − 99.95% = 0.05% = 0.0005, and 10,000,000 × 0.0005 = 5,000. Once 5,000 requests have failed, the budget is spent.

drills.q: Why is the SLA usually set looser than the internal SLO (say SLA 99.5% against an SLO of 99.9%)?
options: So the team is alerted and can fix problems while still inside the SLO, before breaching the contract and owing customers
Because SLAs measure different metrics than SLOs
Because the SLO is for customers and the SLA is internal
drills.explain: The gap is a safety margin. The SLO is the internal target that triggers action; the SLA is the point at which money changes hands. The roles in the last option are reversed.

drills.q: Which SLI best reflects what users feel about a search endpoint's speed?
options: CPU utilisation of the search hosts
Fraction of requests faster than 300 ms (or p99 latency)
drills.explain: Averages hide the slow tail, and a handful of 10-second requests barely move the mean. CPU and QPS describe the system, not the user's experience. A threshold fraction or a high percentile captures the tail.

drills.q: Put the steps of defining and operating an SLO in order.
items: Pick a user journey that matters (e.g. checkout)
Choose the SLI that measures its quality (success ratio, latency under a threshold)
Set a target and a window from user expectations and past data
Spend or protect the remaining budget when deciding about releases
drills.explain: You cannot set a target before you have a metric, nor a metric before you know which user experience matters. Burn-rate alerts and budget-based release decisions only make sense once the SLO exists.
